source: Practice design 2026-11-07 (practice characters, design section 10): the target customer knows only who they are; the student asks one leading and two hypothetical questions

venture.name: ParkSwap
venture.description: Commuter students rent out their reserved campus parking spots by the hour when they are not using them.
venture.segment: Commuter students who drive to campus and park in the paid lots

assumptions.statement: Commuters struggle to find parking before morning classes

evidence.text: 4 of 5 commuters we asked said finding parking makes them late

assumptions.statement: Commuters would pay $5 a month to find a spot faster

turns: Thanks for meeting me. Tell me about the last time you drove to campus for an early class.
Don't you think parking on campus is a total nightmare?
We're building an app where students with reserved spots rent them out by the hour. Would you use it?
Would you pay $5 a month for it?
What did being late cost you that day?
Could I follow up with you next week, and would you introduce me to two other commuters?
good_character: A believable commuter who knows nothing about ParkSwap until Dana describes it: concrete about the last time (when, what happened, what it cost), vague and polite about 'would you use it' and 'would you pay $5' ('maybe', 'it depends'), does not agree just to please, does not volunteer the problem the team hopes for, and never coaches Dana.
good_feedback: Rewards the opening question about the last time and the follow-up on what being late cost; flags 'Don't you think...' as leading and 'Would you use it / pay $5' as hypothetical (what people would do is a guess); credits the request for introductions; lists what the made-up customer said as things to check with real commuters, never as evidence.
note: Fictional venture and people. Only fictional data in evaluation cases.
